## Part C: Alpha opportunity since 2020

```{r C-dispersion, include=FALSE}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
Stocks       <- read_rds("data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds")
Cons         <- read_rds("data/Monthly_Index_Constituents.rds")
Idx_Daily    <- read_rds("data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds")
Implied_Vol  <- read_rds("data/Implied_Vol_Indexes.rds")
Uncertainty  <- read_rds("data/Econ_Uncertainty_Indexes.rds")
Commods      <- read_rds("data/Commodities.rds")
LCL_Cncy_Vol <- read_rds("data/LCL_Currency_Vol_Index.rds")
Gl_Cncy_Vol  <- read_rds("data/Global_Currency_Vol_Index.rds")

YM <- function(x) format(x, "%Y%m")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Weekly constituent returns with benchmark weights
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Weekly frequency, as in Bonus 22 ("less noisy" than daily).
Weekly <-
  Stocks %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(Returns = ifelse(Returns >  0.5,  0.5,          # Bonus 22 winsorising
                   ifelse(Returns < -0.5, -0.5, Returns)),
         YW = format(date, "%Y%W")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, YW) %>%
  summarise(date = dplyr::last(date), Return = prod(1 + Returns) - 1,
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  # one common week-end date so all stocks line up
  group_by(YW) %>% mutate(date = max(date)) %>% ungroup()

# Each week uses the J433 weights published at the PREVIOUS month-end
# (the latest weights an investor would know at that time).
BM_W <-
  Cons %>% filter(Fund == "CappedSWIX") %>%
  transmute(W_YM = YM(date), Tickers, Wt = Weight)

df_stocks <-
  Weekly %>%
  mutate(W_YM = YM(floor_date(date, "month") - days(1))) %>%
  inner_join(BM_W, by = c("W_YM", "Tickers")) %>%
  select(date, Tickers, Return, Wt)

# Benchmark weekly returns (provided Capped SWIX series)
BM_Weekly <-
  Idx_Daily %>% filter(Tickers == "J433") %>%
  mutate(YW = format(date, "%Y%W")) %>%
  group_by(YW) %>%
  summarise(BM = prod(1 + Returns) - 1, .groups = "drop") %>%
  inner_join(Weekly %>% distinct(YW, date), by = "YW") %>%
  select(date, BM)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Cross-sectional volatility (adapted from Bonus 22: Dispersion_Prep)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Weighted CSV  = sqrt( sum_i w_i (R_i - R_BM)^2 )   [question's formula]
# Unweighted    = sqrt( (1/N) sum_i (R_i - R_EW)^2 )
# R_i are rolling NSel-week returns, so dispersion reflects the spread of
# returns over a horizon an active manager actually holds positions.
Dispersion_Prep <- function(df_used, BMUse, NSel = 12, CapDisp = 0.45) {

  df_used %>%
    group_by(Tickers) %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(roll_Rt = RcppRoll::roll_prod(1 + Return, n = NSel, fill = NA,
                                         align = "right") - 1,
           roll_wt = RcppRoll::roll_mean(Wt, n = NSel, fill = NA,
                                         align = "right")) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    left_join(BMUse %>% arrange(date) %>%
                mutate(roll_BM = RcppRoll::roll_prod(1 + BM, n = NSel, fill = NA,
                                                     align = "right") - 1) %>%
                select(date, roll_BM),
              by = "date") %>%
    filter(!is.na(roll_Rt), !is.na(roll_wt), !is.na(roll_BM)) %>%
    group_by(date) %>%
    # re-weight so weights sum to 1 over the stocks available that week
    mutate(roll_wt = roll_wt / sum(roll_wt),
           Idx_U   = mean(roll_Rt)) %>%
    summarise(Dispersion_U = sqrt(mean((roll_Rt - Idx_U)^2)),
              Dispersion_W = sqrt(sum(roll_wt * (roll_Rt - roll_BM)^2)),
              N = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(N_weeks = NSel,
           across(starts_with("Disp"), ~ifelse(. > CapDisp, CapDisp, .)))
}

Disp_12w <- Dispersion_Prep(df_stocks, BM_Weekly, NSel = 12)   # ~3 months
Disp_52w <- Dispersion_Prep(df_stocks, BM_Weekly, NSel = 52)   # ~1 year

g_disp <-
  Disp_12w %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Dispersion_U, Dispersion_W), names_to = "Type", values_to = "Value") %>%
  mutate(Type = ifelse(Type == "Dispersion_W", "Weighted (vs J433)", "Unweighted (vs EW mean)")) %>%
  group_by(Type) %>%
  mutate(Smooth = RcppRoll::roll_mean(Value, n = 12, fill = NA, align = "right")) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ymd(20200101), xmax = max(Disp_12w$date),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(date, Value, color = Type), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(date, Smooth, color = Type), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Cross-sectional volatility of Capped SWIX constituents",
       subtitle = "Rolling 12-week returns; thick line = 12-week average; shaded = since 2020",
       x = "", y = "Dispersion",
       caption = "Note:\nWeekly data, returns winsorised at +/-50% (Bonus 22). Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE) +
  fmxdat::fmx_cols()


# Average dispersion per period
Period_Lab <- function(d) case_when(d <  ymd(20200101) ~ "1. 2015-2019",
                                    d <  ymd(20210101) ~ "2. 2020",
                                    d <  ymd(20240101) ~ "3. 2021-2023",
                                    TRUE               ~ "4. 2024-2026")

Disp_Periods <-
  Disp_12w %>%
  mutate(Period = Period_Lab(date)) %>%
  group_by(Period) %>%
  summarise(Weighted = mean(Dispersion_W), Unweighted = mean(Dispersion_U),
            Avg_Stocks = mean(N), .groups = "drop")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Rolling inter-constituent correlation and PC1 share
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# At each month-end: take the 40 largest J433 constituents (by weight),
# their last 63 trading days (~3 months) of daily returns, and compute
#   (a) average pairwise correlation (equal- and weight-based)
#   (b) share of variance explained by the first principal component
#       of the correlation matrix (Practical 4: eigen()).
# High values = stocks move together = little room for stock picking.
Stocks_C <-
  Stocks %>%
  mutate(Returns = ifelse(Returns >  0.25,  0.25,          # Practical 4 cap
                   ifelse(Returns < -0.25, -0.25, Returns)))

Trade_Dates <- sort(unique(Stocks_C$date))

Month_Ends <-
  Stocks_C %>% distinct(date) %>% mutate(YM = YM(date)) %>%
  group_by(YM) %>% summarise(date = max(date), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20150401))           # need ~3 months of history

Corr_Calc <- function(me_date, me_ym, N_Stocks = 40, N_Days = 63) {

  top <- BM_W %>% filter(W_YM == me_ym) %>% slice_max(Wt, n = N_Stocks)
  if (nrow(top) < 10) return(NULL)

  # the market's last N_Days trading dates (same window for every stock)
  win <- Trade_Dates[Trade_Dates <= me_date] %>% tail(N_Days)

  r <- Stocks_C %>%
    filter(Tickers %in% top$Tickers, date %in% win) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = Tickers, values_from = Returns, id_cols = date) %>%
    select(-date)
  # keep stocks with a full window and some price movement (a suspended
  # stock has zero variance, which makes its correlation undefined)
  r <- r[, colSums(!is.na(r)) == N_Days, drop = FALSE]
  r <- r[, apply(r, 2, sd) > 0, drop = FALSE]

  cm <- cor(r)
  w  <- top %>% filter(Tickers %in% colnames(cm)) %>%
    arrange(match(Tickers, colnames(cm))) %>% pull(Wt)
  w  <- w / sum(w)
  off <- upper.tri(cm)
  ww  <- outer(w, w)

  eval <- eigen(cm, symmetric = TRUE)$values

  tibble(date = me_date,
         Avg_Corr    = mean(cm[off]),
         Avg_Corr_W  = sum(cm[off] * ww[off]) / sum(ww[off]),
         PC1_Share   = eval[1] / sum(eval),
         N           = ncol(cm))
}

Corr_df <-
  map2_df(Month_Ends$date, Month_Ends$YM, ~Corr_Calc(.x, .y))

g_corr <-
  Corr_df %>%
  select(date, `Avg pairwise correlation` = Avg_Corr,
         `Weighted avg correlation` = Avg_Corr_W, `PC1 variance share` = PC1_Share) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "Measure", values_to = "Value") %>%
  ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ymd(20200101), xmax = max(Corr_df$date),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(date, Value, color = Measure), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Co-movement among the 40 largest Capped SWIX stocks",
       subtitle = "Rolling 63-day window, month-end values; shaded = since 2020",
       x = "", y = "",
       caption = "Note:\nPC1 share from eigen-decomposition of the correlation matrix (Practical 4). Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE) +
  fmxdat::fmx_cols()


Corr_Periods <-
  Corr_df %>%
  mutate(Period = Period_Lab(date)) %>%
  group_by(Period) %>%
  summarise(across(c(Avg_Corr, Avg_Corr_W, PC1_Share), mean), .groups = "drop")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. One view of alpha opportunity: dispersion vs correlation (monthly)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
Monthly_Opp <-
  Disp_12w %>%
  mutate(YM = YM(date)) %>%
  group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, Dispersion_W, Dispersion_U) %>%
  inner_join(Corr_df %>% mutate(YM = YM(date)) %>% select(YM, date, Avg_Corr, PC1_Share),
             by = "YM")

g_opp <-
  Monthly_Opp %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20200101)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(Avg_Corr, Dispersion_W)) +
  geom_path(color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(color = year(date)), size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Year") +
  labs(title = "Alpha opportunity map since 2020",
       subtitle = "Bottom-right = stocks move together, little spread; top-left = best for stock pickers",
       x = "Average pairwise correlation (top 40)", y = "Weighted dispersion (12-week)",
       caption = "Note:\nMonth-end values. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Alpha opportunity and global macro drivers (since 2020)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
Levels <-
  bind_rows(Implied_Vol, Uncertainty, LCL_Cncy_Vol %>% select(-Description),
            Gl_Cncy_Vol) %>%
  filter(Ticker %in% c("VIX Index", "VXEEM Index", "EPUCGLCP Index",
                       "MOVE Index", "JPMVXYGL Index", "SAVIUSD Index")) %>%
  mutate(YM = YM(date)) %>%
  group_by(Name, YM) %>%
  summarise(Value = mean(TRI, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

Oil <-
  Commods %>% filter(Ticker == "CO1 Comdty") %>% arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(dlogret = log(TRI) - log(lag(TRI)), YM = YM(date)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(dlogret)) %>%
  group_by(YM) %>%
  summarise(Value = sd(dlogret) * sqrt(252), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Name = "Oil_Brent_RV")

Drivers <- bind_rows(Levels, Oil)

Macro_df <-
  Monthly_Opp %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20200101)) %>%
  inner_join(Drivers, by = "YM")

# (a) Simple correlations
Macro_Cor <-
  Macro_df %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  summarise(Dispersion_W = cor(Dispersion_W, Value),
            Avg_Corr     = cor(Avg_Corr, Value),
            PC1_Share    = cor(PC1_Share, Value),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(Dispersion_W))

# (b) Stratification (Bonus 2): top vs bottom quintile of each driver
Strat <-
  Macro_df %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  mutate(State = case_when(Value >= quantile(Value, 0.8) ~ "High",
                           Value <= quantile(Value, 0.2) ~ "Low",
                           TRUE ~ "Normal")) %>%
  filter(State != "Normal") %>%
  group_by(Name, State) %>%
  summarise(Dispersion_W = mean(Dispersion_W), Avg_Corr = mean(Avg_Corr),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = State, values_from = c(Dispersion_W, Avg_Corr)) %>%
  mutate(Disp_High_vs_Low = Dispersion_W_High / Dispersion_W_Low,
         Corr_High_minus_Low = Avg_Corr_High - Avg_Corr_Low) %>%
  arrange(desc(Disp_High_vs_Low))
```

Weighted dispersion is used as the main measure, for two reasons.

- **It follows the question's formula**, measuring spread around the Capped SWIX.
- **It is the spread that matters to a benchmark-aware manager**, since that manager can only profit from stocks large enough to hold.

The unweighted measure is dominated by small, illiquid names. It also fell after 2020 partly because the index shrank from about 155 to 121 stocks (Table \ref{tab:disp}, Figure \ref{FigC1}).

Weighted dispersion peaked in 2020 (19.6%) and has stayed above its 2015–19 level since (14.4% and 13.8%).

```{r tab-disp, results='asis'}
tab_print(Disp_Periods, caption = "Average 12-week cross-sectional dispersion by period",
          label = "tab:disp")
```

```{r FigC1, fig.cap = "Cross-sectional dispersion of Capped SWIX constituents \\label{FigC1}"}
fmxdat::finplot(g_disp, x.date.dist = "1 year", x.date.type = "%Y",
                x.vert = TRUE, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Correlation among the 40 largest stocks has fallen to its lowest level in the sample (Table \ref{tab:corr}, Figure \ref{FigC2}). The average pairwise correlation is 0.20 in 2024–26, against 0.26 in 2015–19, and the first principal component explains 29% of the variance, against 35%.

```{r tab-corr, results='asis'}
tab_print(Corr_Periods %>% rename(`Avg. correlation` = Avg_Corr, `Weighted avg. correlation` = Avg_Corr_W,
                                  `PC1 share` = PC1_Share),
          caption = "Co-movement among the 40 largest stocks by period", label = "tab:corr")
```

```{r FigC2, fig.cap = "Co-movement among the 40 largest Capped SWIX stocks \\label{FigC2}"}
fmxdat::finplot(g_corr, x.date.dist = "1 year", x.date.type = "%Y",
                x.vert = TRUE, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Together, these measures show that the alpha opportunity has improved since 2020 (Figure \ref{FigC3}).

- **2020 was a false opportunity.** Dispersion was high, but so was correlation: the whole market moved together, and the spread came from volatility rather than stock-specific stories.
- **Since 2021 the market has moved towards the best region for stock pickers**: dispersion above its pre-2020 level, with lower correlation.
- **The pattern recurred briefly in 2025 and 2026**, when correlation jumped during the global shocks identified in Part A.

```{r FigC3, fig.cap = "Alpha opportunity map since 2020: dispersion against correlation \\label{FigC3}"}
fmxdat::finplot(g_opp, x.pct = TRUE, x.pct_acc = 1, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Global macro conditions shape the opportunity set (Tables \ref{tab:macrocor} and \ref{tab:macrostrat}).

- **Global fear raises dispersion and correlation together.** When the VIX, EM implied volatility, oil volatility or rand volatility is in its top quintile:
  - dispersion is 1.3–1.4 times higher than in bottom-quintile months;
  - average correlation is about 0.10 higher.

  The extra spread comes with stocks moving together, so it is harder to exploit.
- **Global policy uncertainty is the exception.** It raises dispersion (1.21 times) with almost no rise in correlation: the only "good" dispersion among the drivers.
- **Bond-market volatility (MOVE) slightly reduces dispersion.**

```{r tab-macrocor, results='asis'}
tab_print(Macro_Cor %>% rename(Driver = Name, Dispersion = Dispersion_W, `Avg. correlation` = Avg_Corr,
                               `PC1 share` = PC1_Share),
          caption = "Correlation of monthly alpha-opportunity measures with global drivers (since 2020)",
          label = "tab:macrocor")
```

```{r tab-macrostrat, results='asis'}
tab_print(Strat %>% rename(Driver = Name) %>%
            select(Driver, `Disp. High` = Dispersion_W_High, `Disp. Low` = Dispersion_W_Low,
                   `Disp. High/Low` = Disp_High_vs_Low, `Corr. High` = Avg_Corr_High,
                   `Corr. Low` = Avg_Corr_Low, `Corr. High - Low` = Corr_High_minus_Low),
          caption = "Dispersion and correlation when each driver is in its top versus bottom quintile (since 2020)",
          label = "tab:macrostrat", size = "\\scriptsize")
```

# Model summary \label{Summary}

```{r tab-summary, results='asis'}
Summary_Tab <- tibble(
  Question = c("A: Has local vol increased?", "A: Does it mirror global?", "A: GJR-GARCH",
               "A: VIX in variance equation", "A: DCC correlation", "A: Offshore drivers",
               "B: SafeCore vs J433", "B: Sources of risk", "B: Factor tilts",
               "C: Alpha opportunity", "C: Macro link"),
  Finding = c("Not structurally; but up sharply in 2026 (20.7% vs 15.0%)",
              "Yes - closest to EM; well above developed markets",
              "Strong leverage effect (gamma > 0, alpha close to 0); half-life about 20 days",
              "Positive and significant: global fear raises local variance",
              "Stable long-run level (about 0.65-0.69), spikes in crises",
              "VXEEM, VIX and oil vol matter; policy-uncertainty indexes do not",
              "Higher return, same vol, smaller drawdown; beta about 1 since 2018",
              "Gold miners: about 20% of weight but 40% of vol; Resources 65% of vol",
              "Momentum, quality, value; no low-vol ballast",
              "Improved since 2020: higher dispersion, lowest correlation",
              "Global fear raises dispersion and correlation together")
)
print(xtable::xtable(Summary_Tab, caption = "Summary of findings", label = "tab:summary",
                     align = c("l", "p{4.2cm}", "p{10cm}")),
      include.rownames = FALSE, comment = FALSE, table.placement = "!htbp",
      caption.placement = "top", size = "\\scriptsize")
```

Table \ref{tab:summary} summarises the findings.

**Part A:**

- Local volatility has not risen structurally since 2015, but it has jumped in 2026 and moves closely with global, and especially emerging-market, volatility.
- The GJR-GARCH models show that volatility responds mainly to bad news.
- The VIX raises local conditional variance directly.
- DCC correlations with global markets rise sharply in crises.
- Offshore market fear and oil volatility separate calm from volatile local months; policy-uncertainty indexes do not.

**Part B:**

- SafeCore has rewarded investors, with higher returns at similar volatility and smaller long-run drawdowns, and has held up reasonably in the worst months.
- It was not built with volatility in mind, and it shows: beta has risen to about one, its risk is concentrated in gold miners, and its factor tilts do not include low volatility.

**Part C:** the opportunity for stock selection has improved since 2020. However, the global shocks that raise local volatility also raise correlation, which reduces the benefit of stock picking exactly when volatility is highest.

**Implications for the team.** The case for building a risk ballast into SafeCore is supported. Three steps would help:

1. **Monitor and cap the risk contribution of the gold miners**, rather than their weight.
2. **Add an explicit low-volatility or defensive tilt**, measured with price-based scores, since the third-party volatility score does not capture volatility.
3. **Treat spikes in the VIX, EM implied volatility and oil volatility as early-warning signals for local risk.**

**Limitations:**

- the short history of the Low Volatility index;
- the monthly frequency of the policy-uncertainty indexes;
- the modest number of extreme months in each stratification;
- currency effects: global indexes are in US dollars, local ones in rand.

QUESTION_2
===============================================================================

# Introduction \label{Introduction}

Size indexes are often treated as interchangeable slices of the same market. They are not. A large-cap index can carry a different sector bet, a different degree of concentration and a different response to market stress than a mid- or small-cap index. For a manager benchmarked to the Capped SWIX (J433), these differences determine whether a size tilt adds diversification or simply re-labels the same risk.

This report studies the JSE Large, Mid and Small cap indexes from January 2015 to September 2026. It asks four questions:

1. How do the indexes differ in sector exposure and stock concentration?
2. How far does each index sit from the Capped SWIX, measured by active share?
3. How do their returns and realised volatility compare, at index and constituent level?
4. Does the ranking of the size indexes change in stressed versus calm months?

The analysis uses stratification, realised and GARCH volatility, rolling returns and active share. Section \ref{Data} describes the data, Section \ref{Method} the methods, Section \ref{Results} the results, and Section \ref{Summary} summarises.

# Data \label{Data}

```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Load data
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Size_Idx  <- read_rds("data/Monthly_Index_Constituents.rds")
Stocks    <- read_rds("data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds")
Idx_Daily <- read_rds("data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds")
Implied   <- read_rds("data/Implied_Vol_Indexes.rds")
Uncert    <- read_rds("data/Econ_Uncertainty_Indexes.rds")
LCL_Cncy  <- read_rds("data/LCL_Currency_Vol_Index.rds")
Commods   <- read_rds("data/Commodities.rds")

# Stock returns start 2015-01-02, so use holdings from end-Dec 2014.
Size_Idx <- Size_Idx %>% filter(date >= ymd(20141231))

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sector map: sector is missing for many (mostly small-cap) rows. Use a
# stock's sector from any other row where it is recorded; otherwise
# label it "Unclassified".
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Sector_Map <-
  Size_Idx %>%
  filter(!is.na(Sector)) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  summarise(Sector_Fill = dplyr::last(Sector))

Size_Idx <-
  Size_Idx %>%
  left_join(Sector_Map, by = "Tickers") %>%
  mutate(Sector = coalesce(Sector, Sector_Fill, "Unclassified")) %>%
  select(-Sector_Fill)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Re-scale weights so each index sums to 1 every month (Bonus 1)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
W_df <-
  Size_Idx %>%
  group_by(Fund, date) %>%
  mutate(weight = Weight / sum(Weight)) %>%
  ungroup()

if (W_df %>% group_by(Fund, date) %>% summarise(s = sum(weight), .groups = "drop") %>%
    filter(abs(s - 1) > 1e-6) %>% nrow() > 0) stop("Weights do not sum to 1")
```

```{r rebuild, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Rebuild daily index returns from holdings
# (Practical 1: rmsfuns::Safe_Return.portfolio, weights as xts)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Index_Builder <- function(Fund_Name) {

  W_xts <- W_df %>% filter(Fund == Fund_Name) %>%
    tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = weight, spread_by = Tickers)

  R_xts <- Stocks %>% filter(Tickers %in% names(W_xts)) %>%
    tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = Returns, spread_by = Tickers)

  # A few holdings have no return data: drop them and re-weight to 1
  W_xts <- W_xts[, names(W_xts) %in% names(R_xts)]
  W_xts[is.na(W_xts)] <- 0
  W_xts <- W_xts / rowSums(W_xts)

  R_xts <- R_xts[, names(W_xts)]
  R_xts[is.na(R_xts)] <- 0

  rmsfuns::Safe_Return.portfolio(R = R_xts, weights = W_xts,
                                 lag_weights = TRUE, geometric = TRUE) %>%
    xts_tbl() %>%
    rename(Returns = portfolio.returns) %>%
    mutate(Tickers = Fund_Name)
}

Rebuilt <- map_df(c("LargeCaps", "MidCaps", "SmallCaps", "CappedSWIX"),
                  Index_Builder)

# Daily log returns used for volatility work throughout
Daily <- Rebuilt %>% mutate(dlogret = log(1 + Returns))

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Validation: rebuilt vs official index series
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Official <-
  Idx_Daily %>%
  filter(Tickers %in% c("J200", "J201", "J202", "J433")) %>%
  mutate(Tickers = recode(Tickers, J200 = "LargeCaps", J201 = "MidCaps",
                          J202 = "SmallCaps", J433 = "CappedSWIX")) %>%
  select(date, Tickers, Official = Returns)

Validation <-
  Rebuilt %>%
  inner_join(Official, by = c("date", "Tickers")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  summarise(Correlation = cor(Returns, Official),
            Ann_Ret_Rebuilt  = prod(1 + Returns)^(252 / n()) - 1,
            Ann_Ret_Official = prod(1 + Official)^(252 / n()) - 1,
            Tracking_Error   = sd(Returns - Official) * sqrt(252))
```

```{r data-tables, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Table: data used
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
fmt <- function(d) format(d, "%b %Y")

Tab_Data <-
  bind_rows(
    Size_Idx %>%
      group_by(Fund) %>%
      summarise(Start = fmt(min(date)), End = fmt(max(date)),
                Detail = paste0("Avg. ", round(n() / n_distinct(date)), " stocks")) %>%
      transmute(Series = paste("Constituents & weights:", Fund),
                Source = "Monthly_Index_Constituents", Frequency = "Monthly",
                Start, End, Detail),
    tibble(Series = "Daily stock returns", Source = "Stock_Returns_Daily",
           Frequency = "Daily", Start = fmt(min(Stocks$date)), End = fmt(max(Stocks$date)),
           Detail = paste(n_distinct(Stocks$Tickers), "stocks")),
    Idx_Daily %>% filter(Tickers %in% c("J200", "J201", "J202", "J433")) %>%
      group_by(Tickers) %>%
      summarise(Start = fmt(min(date)), End = fmt(max(date))) %>%
      transmute(Series = paste("Official index returns:", Tickers),
                Source = "Index_Returns_Daily", Frequency = "Daily", Start, End,
                Detail = "Validation"),
    bind_rows(Implied %>% filter(Name == "VIX"),
              Uncert %>% filter(Name == "EPUCGLCP"),
              LCL_Cncy %>% select(-Description),
              Commods %>% filter(Ticker == "CO1 Comdty")) %>%
      group_by(Name) %>%
      summarise(Start = fmt(min(date)), End = fmt(max(date))) %>%
      transmute(Series = recode(Name, VIX = "VIX (US implied vol)",
                                EPUCGLCP = "Global policy uncertainty (EPU)",
                                SAVIUSD = "Rand implied vol (SAVIUSD)",
                                Oil_Brent = "Brent crude (realised vol)"),
                Source = "Macro series", Frequency = "Daily/monthly", Start, End,
                Detail = "Stratification")
  )

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Table: descriptive statistics of daily returns
# Jarque-Bera normality test: JB = n/6 * (S^2 + K^2 / 4) ~ chi2(2)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Tab_Desc <-
  Daily %>%
  group_by(Index = Tickers) %>%
  summarise(Obs               = n(),
            `Mean (ann.)`     = mean(dlogret) * 252,
            `SD (ann.)`       = sd(dlogret) * sqrt(252),
            Skewness          = PerformanceAnalytics::skewness(dlogret),
            `Excess kurtosis` = PerformanceAnalytics::kurtosis(dlogret, method = "excess"),
            Min               = min(Returns),
            Max               = max(Returns),
            `Jarque-Bera p`   = 1 - pchisq(n() / 6 * (Skewness^2 + `Excess kurtosis`^2 / 4), df = 2)) %>%
  mutate(Index = factor(Index, levels = c("LargeCaps", "MidCaps", "SmallCaps", "CappedSWIX"))) %>%
  arrange(Index) %>%
  mutate(Index = as.character(Index))
```

Table \ref{tab:data} lists the data. Monthly constituent weights for the three size indexes and the Capped SWIX come from the index constituents file. They are combined with daily returns for 277 JSE stocks to rebuild each index, which lets us look inside the indexes rather than only at their headline returns. The official index series (J200, J201, J202, J433) are used only to check the rebuild. Four macro series are used for stratification.

```{r tab-data, results='asis'}
tab_print(Tab_Data, caption = "Data used", label = "tab:data", size = "\\scriptsize")
```

Three data treatments matter:

- **Missing sectors.** Sector labels are missing for many small-cap rows. Each stock is given the sector recorded for it elsewhere in the data; stocks with no record are labelled "Unclassified". This affects about 30% of small-cap weight before 2020 and about 10% afterwards.
- **Weights.** Weights are rescaled to sum to one each month, after dropping the few holdings without return data.
- **Returns.** For stock-level volatility, daily stock returns are capped at $\pm 25\%$ to limit data errors.

Table \ref{tab:valid} shows that the rebuilt indexes track the official series closely: daily correlations of 0.98 to 0.99, and annualised returns within 0.3 percentage points.

```{r tab-valid, results='asis'}
tab_print(Validation %>% rename(Index = Tickers, `Ann. return (rebuilt)` = Ann_Ret_Rebuilt,
                                `Ann. return (official)` = Ann_Ret_Official,
                                `Tracking error` = Tracking_Error),
          caption = "Validation: rebuilt versus official index returns (daily)",
          label = "tab:valid")
```

Table \ref{tab:desc} reports descriptive statistics of the rebuilt daily returns. All four series are negatively skewed and fat-tailed, and normality is rejected for each (Jarque–Bera $p<0.001$). Small caps stand out: the lowest daily volatility, but by far the fattest tails (excess kurtosis of 23). That combination is the first hint that daily small-cap volatility understates their true risk (Section \ref{Vol}).

```{r tab-desc, results='asis'}
tab_print(Tab_Desc,
          caption = "Descriptive statistics of daily index returns (Jan 2015 to Sep 2026)",
          label = "tab:desc")
```

# Methodology \label{Method}

## Index returns

Each index return is built from its constituents. With $w_{i,t-1}$ the weight of stock $i$ at the previous month-end, and weights drifting with prices within the month:

$$
R_{p,t} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_{i,t-1} \, R_{i,t}, \qquad \sum_i w_{i,t-1} = 1.
$$

This is implemented with `rmsfuns::Safe_Return.portfolio`, as in the course practicals.

## Concentration and active share

Concentration is measured by the top-10 weight and by the effective number of stocks, the inverse of the Herfindahl–Hirschman index:

$$
N^{\text{eff}}_t = \frac{1}{\sum_i w_{i,t}^2}.
$$

$N^{\text{eff}}$ is the number of equally weighted stocks that would give the same concentration.

Active share measures how much of an index's holdings differ from the benchmark [@cremers2009]:

$$
AS_t = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i} \left| w^{\text{index}}_{i,t} - w^{\text{J433}}_{i,t} \right|.
$$

It runs from 0 (identical holdings) to 1 (no overlap).

## Rolling returns and realised volatility

The rolling three-year annualised return is

$$
R^{(36)}_t = \Big(\prod_{s=t-35}^{t} (1+R_s)\Big)^{12/36} - 1.
$$

Realised volatility uses daily log returns $r_t = \ln(1+R_t)$:

$$
\sigma^{RV}_t = \sqrt{252} \cdot \text{sd}\left(r_{t-251}, \dots, r_t\right).
$$

At constituent level, each stock's realised volatility is computed per calendar year. The diversification ratio compares index volatility with the average volatility of its stocks:

$$
DR = \frac{\sigma_{\text{index}}}{\sum_i \bar{w}_i \, \sigma_i}.
$$

A low $DR$ means combining the stocks removes much of their individual risk.

## GJR-GARCH model

Volatility is also modelled with a GJR-GARCH(1,1) [@glosten1993], which lets bad news raise volatility more than good news:

$$
r_t = \mu + \phi\, r_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \sim t_\nu,
$$
$$
\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \left(\alpha + \gamma\, I_{t-1}\right)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta\,\sigma_{t-1}^2, \qquad I_{t-1} = \begin{cases} 1 & \varepsilon_{t-1} < 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
$$

- $\gamma > 0$ is the leverage effect.
- Persistence is $\alpha + \beta + \gamma/2$, and the half-life of a volatility shock is $\ln(0.5)/\ln(\text{persistence})$ days.
- Student-$t$ errors allow for the fat tails in Table \ref{tab:desc}.
- Adequacy is checked with a Ljung–Box test on squared standardised residuals.

## Stale prices

Infrequent trading smooths measured returns [@scholes1977; @lo1990]. Three indicators are used:

- the share of zero-return days;
- the first-order autocorrelation of daily returns;
- the ratio of volatility from monthly returns to volatility from daily returns ($\text{sd}(R^{m})\sqrt{12} \,/\, \text{sd}(R^{d})\sqrt{252}$). With serially independent returns this ratio is close to one; stale prices push it above one.

## Stratification

Following the course's stratification approach, months are sorted by a stratifying series $X_m$: J433 realised volatility, VIX, rand implied volatility, oil realised volatility and global policy uncertainty. High (low) months are the top (bottom) quintile of $X_m$. Daily returns are winsorised at the 1st and 99th percentiles. For each index:

- the volatility ratio is $\sigma_{\text{High}}/\sigma_{\text{Full}}$;
- the monthly excess return over J433 is compared between High and Low months with a Welch two-sample $t$-test.

# Results \label{Results}

## Sector exposure

```{r sector, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sector exposure over time (Practical 2 / Bonus 2: weights from holdings)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Sector_W <-
  W_df %>%
  group_by(Fund, date, Sector) %>%
  summarise(Weight = sum(weight), .groups = "drop")

g_sector <-
  Sector_W %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_area(aes(date, Weight, fill = Sector), alpha = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(~Fund, nrow = 1) +
  labs(title = "Sector exposure of the size indexes",
       subtitle = "Re-scaled month-end constituent weights",
       x = "", y = "Weight",
       caption = "Note:\nUnclassified = no sector recorded in the data. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE) +
  fmxdat::fmx_fills()

# Average sector weights by period
Sector_Table <-
  Sector_W %>%
  mutate(Period = ifelse(date < ymd(20200101), "2015-2019", "2020-2026")) %>%
  group_by(Fund, Period, Sector) %>%
  summarise(Weight = mean(Weight), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Sector, values_from = Weight, values_fill = 0)

# Largest holdings at the latest date (used in the text)
Top_Now <-
  W_df %>% filter(date == max(date), Fund != "CappedSWIX") %>%
  group_by(Fund) %>% slice_max(weight, n = 5) %>%
  select(Fund, Tickers, Sector, weight)
```

The three indexes carry very different sector bets (Figure \ref{Figure1}, Table \ref{tab:sector}).

- **Large caps carry the market's Resources risk.** Resources rose from about 20% of the index in 2015–19 to 35–40% by 2026, led by the gold miners; Gold Fields and AngloGold Ashanti are now the two largest holdings.
- **Mid caps have shifted from Property towards Financials**, with Financials more than doubling, from 12% to 28%.
- **Small caps are effectively a Property and Industrials index**, with little exposure to Resources or Financials.

```{r Figure1, fig.cap = "Sector exposure of the size indexes \\label{Figure1}", fig.height = 4.2}
fmxdat::finplot(g_sector, x.date.dist = "2 years", x.date.type = "%Y",
                x.vert = TRUE, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

```{r tab-sector, results='asis'}
tab_print(Sector_Table %>% rename(Index = Fund),
          caption = "Average sector weights by period", label = "tab:sector",
          size = "\\scriptsize")
```

## Concentration

```{r concentration, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Concentration: number of stocks, top-10 weight, effective N = 1 / HHI
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Concentration <-
  W_df %>%
  group_by(Fund, date) %>%
  arrange(desc(weight), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(N = n(),
            Top10 = sum(head(weight, 10)),
            HHI = sum(weight^2),
            Eff_N = 1 / HHI, .groups = "drop")

g_conc <-
  Concentration %>%
  select(date, Fund, `Top-10 weight` = Top10, `Effective N` = Eff_N) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(`Top-10 weight`, `Effective N`)) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, value, color = Fund), linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Stock concentration of the size indexes",
       x = "", y = "",
       caption = "Note:\nEffective N = 1 / sum of squared weights. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE) +
  fmxdat::fmx_cols()

Conc_Table <-
  Concentration %>%
  mutate(Period = case_when(date < ymd(20200101) ~ "1. 2015-2019",
                            date < ymd(20240101) ~ "2. 2020-2023",
                            TRUE ~ "3. 2024-2026")) %>%
  group_by(Fund, Period) %>%
  summarise(across(c(N, Top10, Eff_N), mean), .groups = "drop")
```

Large caps are the most concentrated index (Figure \ref{Figure2}, Table \ref{tab:conc}). Until mid-2023, ten stocks held about two-thirds of the index ($N^{\text{eff}} \approx 14$). A clear break in mid-2023 lowered the top-10 weight to about 55%. Its cause is not visible in the data; a change in index methodology or capping is one possibility.

Mid caps have moved the other way. Their effective number of stocks fell from 38 to 27, so mid-cap returns now rest on fewer names. Small caps remain the most diversified.

```{r Figure2, fig.cap = "Stock concentration: top-10 weight and effective number of stocks \\label{Figure2}"}
fmxdat::finplot(g_conc, x.date.dist = "2 years", x.date.type = "%Y", x.vert = TRUE)
```

```{r tab-conc, results='asis'}
tab_print(Conc_Table %>% rename(Index = Fund, `Stocks (N)` = N, `Top-10 weight` = Top10,
                                `Effective N` = Eff_N),
          caption = "Concentration by period (averages)", label = "tab:conc", digits = 2)
```

## Active share relative to the Capped SWIX

```{r active-share, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Active share (Cremers & Petajisto, 2009): 0.5 * sum |w_index - w_J433|
# 0 = identical to the benchmark; 1 = no overlap at all.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
BM_W <- W_df %>% filter(Fund == "CappedSWIX") %>%
  select(date, Tickers, w_bm = weight)

Active_Share <-
  W_df %>%
  filter(Fund != "CappedSWIX") %>%
  select(date, Fund, Tickers, w_idx = weight) %>%
  group_by(Fund) %>%
  group_modify(~ full_join(.x, BM_W, by = c("date", "Tickers"))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(across(c(w_idx, w_bm), ~replace_na(., 0))) %>%
  group_by(Fund, date) %>%
  summarise(Active_Share = 0.5 * sum(abs(w_idx - w_bm)),
            # share of the benchmark held by the index
            BM_Coverage = sum(w_bm[w_idx > 0]), .groups = "drop")

g_as <-
  Active_Share %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Active_Share, color = Fund), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Active share of the size indexes vs the Capped SWIX",
       x = "", y = "Active share",
       caption = "Note:\nActive share = 0.5 x sum of absolute weight differences. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE) +
  fmxdat::fmx_cols()

AS_Table <-
  Active_Share %>%
  mutate(Period = case_when(date < ymd(20200101) ~ "1. 2015-2019",
                            date < ymd(20240101) ~ "2. 2020-2023",
                            TRUE ~ "3. 2024-2026")) %>%
  group_by(Fund, Period) %>%
  summarise(across(c(Active_Share, BM_Coverage), mean), .groups = "drop")

# Overlap between size indexes (stocks held in two indexes at once)
Overlap <-
  W_df %>% filter(Fund != "CappedSWIX") %>%
  group_by(date, Tickers) %>% filter(n() > 1) %>%
  summarise(Funds = paste(sort(Fund), collapse = " & "), .groups = "drop") %>%
  count(date, Funds) %>% group_by(Funds) %>%
  summarise(Months = n(), Avg_Stocks = mean(n), Max_Stocks = max(n))
```

Large caps are increasingly close to the benchmark (Figure \ref{Figure3}, Table \ref{tab:as}). Their active share halved, from 29% in 2015–19 to 15% in 2024–26. A large-cap tilt therefore adds little that is different from J433.

Mid and small caps are genuinely different portfolios, with active shares of about 75% and 93%. Small caps hold stocks that make up only about 7% of the Capped SWIX, which makes them a true diversifier relative to the benchmark.

One data feature is worth noting: in most months, about 12 stocks sit in both the large- and mid-cap indexes at the same time, with a small large-cap weight. This appears to reflect stocks migrating between size bands; the weights are used as given.

```{r Figure3, fig.cap = "Active share of the size indexes relative to the Capped SWIX \\label{Figure3}"}
fmxdat::finplot(g_as, x.date.dist = "1 year", x.date.type = "%Y",
                x.vert = TRUE, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

```{r tab-as, results='asis'}
tab_print(AS_Table %>% rename(Index = Fund, `Active share` = Active_Share,
                              `Share of J433 weight held` = BM_Coverage),
          caption = "Active share relative to the Capped SWIX", label = "tab:as")
```

## Risk and return

```{r moments, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Monthly returns and statistics table (Bonus 12: Moments_Comp)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Monthly_Ret <-
  Daily %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, YM) %>%
  summarise(date = dplyr::last(date), Ret = prod(1 + Returns) - 1,
            .groups = "drop")

Moments_Comp <- function(funds, BM, Yrs_LookBack) {

  funds_considered <-
    funds %>% filter(date >= fmxdat::safe_year_min(datesel = dplyr::last(date),
                                                    N = Yrs_LookBack))

  Fundxts <- funds_considered %>%
    tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = Ret, spread_by = Tickers, Colnames_Exact = TRUE)
  BMxts   <- funds_considered %>% filter(Tickers == BM) %>%
    tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = Ret, Colnames_Exact = TRUE)

  # Forces every statistic into one row (one column per index)
  one_row <- function(x) {
    x <- as.matrix(x)
    if (nrow(x) > 1) x <- t(x)
    out <- data.frame(x)
    colnames(out) <- colnames(Fundxts)
    out
  }

  bind_rows(
    one_row(Return.cumulative(Fundxts)),
    one_row(Return.annualized(Fundxts, scale = 12, geometric = TRUE)),
    one_row(Return.annualized.excess(Fundxts, BMxts)),
    one_row(sd.annualized(Fundxts, scale = 12, geometric = TRUE)),
    one_row(SharpeRatio.annualized(Fundxts, Rf = 0, scale = 12)),
    one_row(maxDrawdown(Fundxts)),
    one_row(PainIndex(Fundxts, scale = 12, geometric = TRUE)),
    one_row(fmxdat::Safe_TE(Ra = Fundxts, Rb = BMxts, scale = 12)),
    one_row(CAPM.beta(Ra = Fundxts, Rb = BMxts, Rf = 0)),
    one_row(UpDownRatios(Ra = Fundxts, Rb = BMxts, method = "Capture", side = "Up")),
    one_row(UpDownRatios(Ra = Fundxts, Rb = BMxts, method = "Capture", side = "Down")),
    one_row(CVaR(R = Fundxts, p = 0.95, method = "modified"))
  ) %>%
    mutate(Period = glue::glue("Last {Yrs_LookBack} Years"),
           Info = c("Cum Returns", "Returns (Ann.)", "Returns Excess (Ann.)",
                    "SD (Ann.)", "Return / Risk", "Max Drawdown", "Pain Index",
                    "Tracking Error", "Beta", "Up Capture", "Down Capture",
                    "Modified CVaR (95%, monthly)")) %>%
    relocate(Period, Info) %>%
    as_tibble()
}

Tab_stats <-
  bind_rows(
    Moments_Comp(Monthly_Ret, BM = "CappedSWIX", Yrs_LookBack = 3),
    Moments_Comp(Monthly_Ret, BM = "CappedSWIX", Yrs_LookBack = 5),
    Moments_Comp(Monthly_Ret, BM = "CappedSWIX", Yrs_LookBack = 10)
  )
```

Table \ref{tab:stats} compares the indexes over the last ten years using monthly returns.

- **Large caps** delivered the best balance of return and risk: 11.6% a year, a 22.6% maximum drawdown and a beta of about one.
- **Small caps** matched that return (11.4%) with a beta of only 0.73, but suffered the deepest drawdown (41.5%).
- **Mid caps** lagged, at 6.9% a year.

```{r tab-stats, results='asis'}
tab_print(Tab_stats %>% filter(Period == "Last 10 Years") %>% select(-Period) %>%
            select(Info, LargeCaps, MidCaps, SmallCaps, CappedSWIX),
          caption = "Risk and return statistics, last 10 years (monthly returns, benchmark J433)",
          label = "tab:stats")
```

```{r rolling-returns, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Rolling 3-year annualised returns (Practical 1: RcppRoll::roll_prod)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Roll_Ret <-
  Monthly_Ret %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(RollRets = RcppRoll::roll_prod(1 + Ret, n = 36, fill = NA,
                                        align = "right")^(12 / 36) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(RollRets))

g_rollret <-
  Roll_Ret %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, RollRets, color = Tickers), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Rolling 3-year annualised returns: size indexes",
       x = "", y = "Annualised return",
       caption = "Note:\nIndexes rebuilt from constituents. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE) +
  fmxdat::fmx_cols()

# How often did each index beat the Capped SWIX over 3-year windows?
Roll_Win <-
  Roll_Ret %>%
  select(date, Tickers, RollRets) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Tickers, values_from = RollRets) %>%
  summarise(across(c(LargeCaps, MidCaps, SmallCaps),
                   list(Beat_BM = ~mean(. > CappedSWIX),
                        Avg_Gap = ~mean(. - CappedSWIX))))
```

Rolling three-year returns (Figure \ref{Figure4}) show how consistent these outcomes were.

- **Large caps beat the Capped SWIX in 96% of three-year windows**, by about 2.5% a year on average.
- **Small caps won 64% of the time but swung widely**, from $-16\%$ a year in 2019–20 to about 37% in 2022–23.
- **Mid caps beat the benchmark in only 26% of windows.**

```{r Figure4, fig.cap = "Rolling three-year annualised returns \\label{Figure4}"}
fmxdat::finplot(g_rollret, x.date.dist = "1 year", x.date.type = "%Y",
                x.vert = TRUE, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

## Realised volatility \label{Vol}

```{r rolling-vol, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Rolling 1-year realised volatility (Practical 1: RcppRoll::roll_sd)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Roll_SD <-
  Daily %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(RollSD = RcppRoll::roll_sd(dlogret, n = 252, fill = NA,
                                    align = "right") * sqrt(252)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(RollSD))

g_rollsd <-
  Roll_SD %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, RollSD, color = Tickers), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Rolling 1-year realised volatility: size indexes",
       x = "", y = "Annualised SD",
       caption = "Note:\nDaily log returns, 252-day window. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE) +
  fmxdat::fmx_cols()
```

At index level, all three size indexes became much more volatile in 2020 (about 29–32%), then settled (Figure \ref{Figure5}). Small caps were consistently the calmest on daily data: about 12% since 2024, against 17% for large and mid caps.

```{r Figure5, fig.cap = "Rolling one-year realised volatility \\label{Figure5}"}
fmxdat::finplot(g_rollsd, x.date.dist = "1 year", x.date.type = "%Y",
                x.vert = TRUE, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

```{r constituent-vol, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Realised volatility of the CONSTITUENTS
# a) Yearly realised vol per stock. Daily returns capped at +-25% to limit
#    data errors; a stock needs >= 100 trading days in the year.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Stock_RV <-
  Stocks %>%
  mutate(Returns = pmin(pmax(Returns, -0.25), 0.25),
         dlogret = log(1 + Returns), Year = year(date)) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, Year) %>%
  summarise(RV = sd(dlogret, na.rm = TRUE) * sqrt(252),
            N_days = sum(!is.na(dlogret)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(N_days >= 100)

# b) Assign each stock to ONE size index per year: the index it sat in for
#    most months (ties: the larger average weight).
Membership <-
  Size_Idx %>%
  filter(Fund != "CappedSWIX", date >= ymd(20150101)) %>%
  mutate(Year = year(date)) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, Year, Fund) %>%
  summarise(Months = n(), Avg_W = mean(Weight), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(Tickers, Year) %>%
  arrange(desc(Months), desc(Avg_W), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup()

Const_RV <- inner_join(Membership, Stock_RV, by = c("Tickers", "Year"))

g_constrv <-
  Const_RV %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_boxplot(aes(factor(Year), RV, fill = Fund), outlier.alpha = 0.3,
               outlier.size = 0.8) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Realised volatility of index constituents, by year",
       subtitle = "Each box = distribution of stock-level annualised volatility",
       x = "", y = "Annualised SD",
       caption = "Note:\nStocks assigned to the size index they sat in for most of the year. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE) +
  fmxdat::fmx_fills()

# c) Typical stock vol vs index vol: the diversification ratio
Const_Summary <-
  Const_RV %>%
  group_by(Fund, Year) %>%
  summarise(Median_Stock_RV = median(RV),
            WAvg_Stock_RV   = weighted.mean(RV, Avg_W),
            IQR_Stock_RV    = IQR(RV), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(Daily %>% mutate(Year = year(date)) %>%
              group_by(Tickers, Year) %>%
              summarise(Index_RV = sd(dlogret) * sqrt(252), .groups = "drop"),
            by = c("Fund" = "Tickers", "Year")) %>%
  mutate(Div_Ratio = Index_RV / WAvg_Stock_RV)

Const_Period <-
  Const_Summary %>%
  mutate(Period = case_when(Year < 2020 ~ "1. 2015-2019",
                            Year == 2020 ~ "2. 2020",
                            Year < 2024 ~ "3. 2021-2023",
                            TRUE ~ "4. 2024-2026")) %>%
  group_by(Fund, Period) %>%
  summarise(across(c(Median_Stock_RV, WAvg_Stock_RV, IQR_Stock_RV,
                     Index_RV, Div_Ratio), mean), .groups = "drop")
```

The constituent view reverses this picture (Figure \ref{Figure6}, Table \ref{tab:const}).

- **Individual small-cap stocks are the most volatile** (median of about 36% in 2015–19, against 28% for large caps).
- **Yet the small-cap index is the calmest**, because its stocks move largely independently. Its diversification ratio is 0.28–0.41, against about 0.5 for large and mid caps.
- **In 2020 the ratio rose sharply**: stocks moved together and diversification disappeared when it was needed most.

```{r Figure6, fig.cap = "Distribution of constituent realised volatility by year \\label{Figure6}", fig.height = 4.2}
fmxdat::finplot(g_constrv, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

```{r tab-const, results='asis'}
tab_print(Const_Period %>% rename(Index = Fund, `Median stock vol` = Median_Stock_RV,
                                  `Wtd. avg. stock vol` = WAvg_Stock_RV,
                                  `IQR stock vol` = IQR_Stock_RV, `Index vol` = Index_RV,
                                  `Diversification ratio` = Div_Ratio),
          caption = "Constituent versus index realised volatility", label = "tab:const",
          size = "\\scriptsize")
```

```{r stale, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Stale-price check: is small-cap volatility understated?
# Illiquid stocks often do not trade, so their price is unchanged for the
# day. This smooths daily returns (low daily vol, positive autocorrelation),
# so vol from MONTHLY returns exceeds daily vol x sqrt(252).
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Stale_Check <-
  Daily %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  summarise(AC1_daily = cor(Returns, dplyr::lag(Returns), use = "complete.obs"),
            SD_from_daily = sd(Returns) * sqrt(252)) %>%
  left_join(Monthly_Ret %>% group_by(Tickers) %>%
              summarise(SD_from_monthly = sd(Ret) * sqrt(12)), by = "Tickers") %>%
  mutate(Ratio = SD_from_monthly / SD_from_daily)

# Share of zero-return days for the stocks in each size index
Zero_Days <-
  Stocks %>%
  inner_join(Membership %>% distinct(Tickers, Fund), by = "Tickers",
             relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  group_by(Fund) %>%
  summarise(Zero_Return_Days = mean(Returns == 0, na.rm = TRUE))

Stale_Table <-
  Stale_Check %>%
  left_join(Zero_Days, by = c("Tickers" = "Fund"))
```

Part of the small caps' calm is, however, an illusion (Table \ref{tab:stale}).

- Small-cap stocks do not trade on about 11% of days.
- Small-cap daily index returns are positively autocorrelated.
- Volatility measured on monthly returns is higher than on daily returns (ratio 1.06); for large caps the ratio is 0.80.

These are the signatures of stale prices. Daily small-cap volatility understates true risk, which is consistent with the fat tails in Table \ref{tab:desc} and the 41.5% drawdown.

```{r tab-stale, results='asis'}
tab_print(Stale_Table %>% rename(Index = Tickers, `AC(1) daily` = AC1_daily,
                                 `SD from daily` = SD_from_daily,
                                 `SD from monthly` = SD_from_monthly,
                                 `Monthly / daily` = Ratio,
                                 `Zero-return days` = Zero_Return_Days),
          caption = "Stale-price diagnostics", label = "tab:stale")
```

```{r garch, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# GJR-GARCH(1,1), AR(1) mean, Student-t errors (Practical 6: rugarch)
# Same specification as Q1A.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
garch_spec <-
  ugarchspec(variance.model = list(model = "gjrGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
             mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(1, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
             distribution.model = "std")

Garch_Fitter <- function(df, Ticker_Sel, spec) {
  x <- df %>% filter(Tickers == Ticker_Sel) %>% tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = dlogret)
  ugarchfit(spec = spec, data = x)
}

Idx_Names <- c("LargeCaps", "MidCaps", "SmallCaps", "CappedSWIX")
Fits <- map(Idx_Names, ~Garch_Fitter(Daily, .x, garch_spec)) %>%
  set_names(Idx_Names)

# Diagnostics: squared standardised residuals should show no ARCH left
LB_p <- map_dbl(Fits, ~Box.test(residuals(.x, standardize = TRUE)^2,
                                type = "Ljung-Box", lag = 12)$p.value)

# Key parameters side by side
Garch_Table <-
  map_df(Idx_Names, function(nm) {
    cf <- coef(Fits[[nm]])
    tibble(Index = nm, alpha = cf["alpha1"], beta = cf["beta1"],
           gamma = cf["gamma1"], gamma_p = Fits[[nm]]@fit$matcoef["gamma1", 4],
           shape = cf["shape"], Persistence = persistence(Fits[[nm]]),
           Half_Life_days = log(0.5) / log(persistence(Fits[[nm]])),
           LB_sq_p = LB_p[[nm]])
  })

Sigma_df <-
  map_df(Idx_Names, function(nm) {
    sigma(Fits[[nm]]) %>% xts_tbl() %>%
      purrr::set_names(c("date", "sigma")) %>%
      mutate(date = as.Date(date), Tickers = nm)
  }) %>%
  mutate(Ann_Sigma = sigma * sqrt(252))

g_sigma <-
  Sigma_df %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Ann_Sigma, color = Tickers), linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(title = "GJR-GARCH(1,1) conditional volatility: size indexes",
       x = "", y = "Annualised conditional SD",
       caption = "Note:\nAR(1) mean, Student-t errors. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE) +
  fmxdat::fmx_cols()
```

The GJR-GARCH estimates (Table \ref{tab:garch}, Figure \ref{Figure7}) add a further difference.

- **Large-cap volatility reacts almost only to bad news** ($\alpha \approx 0$, $\gamma = 0.15$), like the Capped SWIX.
- **Small and mid caps respond more symmetrically** (higher $\alpha$, lower $\gamma$). Their volatility is driven more by stock-specific news than by market sell-offs.
- **Shocks fade quickly** in all indexes, with half-lives of 12–18 trading days.
- **The models are adequate**: none of the Ljung–Box tests on squared standardised residuals rejects ($p$ = 0.35 to 0.99).

```{r Figure7, fig.cap = "GJR-GARCH(1,1) conditional volatility \\label{Figure7}"}
fmxdat::finplot(g_sigma, x.date.dist = "1 year", x.date.type = "%Y",
                x.vert = TRUE, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

## Stratification: calm versus stressed months

```{r stratification, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Stratification (Bonus 2): monthly buckets, returns winsorised at 1%/99%,
# extreme months = top / bottom quintile of each stratifying series.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Idxs <-
  Rebuilt %>%
  rename(Return = Returns) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Top = quantile(Return, 0.99), Bot = quantile(Return, 0.01)) %>%
  mutate(Return = ifelse(Return > Top, Top,
                         ifelse(Return < Bot, Bot, Return))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(date, Tickers, Return) %>%
  mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m"))

# (a) Local market stress: the Capped SWIX's own realised vol each month
J433_RV <-
  Idxs %>% filter(Tickers == "CappedSWIX") %>%
  group_by(YearMonth) %>%
  summarise(Value = sd(Return) * sqrt(252), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Name = "J433 realised vol")

# (b) Levels: rand implied vol (SAVIUSD), VIX, global policy uncertainty
Levels <-
  bind_rows(Implied, Uncert, LCL_Cncy %>% select(-Description)) %>%
  filter(Ticker %in% c("VIX Index", "EPUCGLCP Index", "SAVIUSD Index")) %>%
  mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m"),
         Name = recode(Name, SAVIUSD = "Rand implied vol (SAVIUSD)",
                       VIX = "VIX", EPUCGLCP = "Global policy uncertainty")) %>%
  group_by(Name, YearMonth) %>%
  summarise(Value = mean(TRI, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# (c) Oil: Brent is a price, so use its monthly realised volatility
Oil_RV <-
  Commods %>%
  filter(Ticker == "CO1 Comdty") %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(dlogret = log(TRI) - log(lag(TRI))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(dlogret)) %>%
  mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>%
  group_by(YearMonth) %>%
  summarise(Value = sd(dlogret) * sqrt(252), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Name = "Oil realised vol")

# Keep months in the index sample only, then define quintiles
Strat <-
  bind_rows(J433_RV, Levels, Oil_RV) %>%
  filter(YearMonth %in% unique(Idxs$YearMonth)) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  mutate(TopQtile = quantile(Value, 0.8),
         BotQtile = quantile(Value, 0.2)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Perf_comparisons (Bonus 2): SD in extreme months vs full-sample SD
Perf_comparisons <- function(Idxs, YMs, Alias) {
  Idxs %>%
    group_by(Tickers) %>%
    mutate(Full_SD = sd(Return) * sqrt(252)) %>%
    filter(YearMonth %in% YMs) %>%
    summarise(SD = sd(Return) * sqrt(252),
              across(.cols = starts_with("Full"), .fns = max)) %>%
    arrange(desc(SD)) %>%
    mutate(Period = Alias) %>%
    group_by(Tickers) %>%
    mutate(Ratio = SD / Full_SD) %>%
    ungroup()
}

SD_Results <-
  map_df(unique(Strat$Name), function(nm) {
    Hi_Vol  <- Strat %>% filter(Name == nm, Value > TopQtile) %>% pull(YearMonth)
    Low_Vol <- Strat %>% filter(Name == nm, Value < BotQtile) %>% pull(YearMonth)
    bind_rows(Perf_comparisons(Idxs, YMs = Hi_Vol,  Alias = "High"),
              Perf_comparisons(Idxs, YMs = Low_Vol, Alias = "Low")) %>%
      mutate(Stratifier = nm)
  })

# Returns in extreme months, relative to the Capped SWIX
Monthly_W <-
  Idxs %>%
  group_by(Tickers, YearMonth) %>%
  summarise(Ret = prod(1 + Return) - 1, .groups = "drop")

Excess <-
  Monthly_W %>%
  left_join(Monthly_W %>% filter(Tickers == "CappedSWIX") %>%
              select(YearMonth, BM = Ret), by = "YearMonth") %>%
  filter(Tickers != "CappedSWIX") %>%
  mutate(Excess = Ret - BM)

Ret_Results <-
  Excess %>%
  inner_join(Strat, by = "YearMonth", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  mutate(State = case_when(Value > TopQtile ~ "High",
                           Value < BotQtile ~ "Low",
                           TRUE ~ "Middle")) %>%
  filter(State != "Middle") %>%
  group_by(Stratifier = Name, Tickers, State) %>%
  summarise(Months = n(),
            Avg_Ret = mean(Ret),
            Avg_Excess = mean(Excess),
            Hit_Rate = mean(Excess > 0), .groups = "drop")

# Welch two-sample t-test: excess return in High vs Low months
T_Tests <-
  Excess %>%
  inner_join(Strat, by = "YearMonth", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  mutate(State = case_when(Value > TopQtile ~ "High",
                           Value < BotQtile ~ "Low", TRUE ~ NA_character_)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(State)) %>%
  group_by(Stratifier = Name, Tickers) %>%
  summarise(Diff_Hi_minus_Lo = mean(Excess[State == "High"]) - mean(Excess[State == "Low"]),
            p_value = t.test(Excess[State == "High"], Excess[State == "Low"])$p.value,
            .groups = "drop")

g_strat <-
  Ret_Results %>%
  mutate(State = factor(State, levels = c("Low", "High"))) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_col(aes(Tickers, Avg_Excess, fill = State), position = "dodge") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~Stratifier, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 14)) +
  labs(title = "Size indexes in calm vs stressed months",
       subtitle = "High / Low = top / bottom quintile of each series",
       x = "", y = "Avg monthly excess return",
       caption = "Note:\nDaily returns winsorised at 1% / 99%. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE) +
  fmxdat::fmx_fills() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))
```

Every size index becomes much more volatile in stressed months (Table \ref{tab:stratsd}), so size offers no shelter from volatility. Small caps react most to global fear (VIX), and mid caps least to local stress. Global policy uncertainty barely changes volatility.

```{r tab-stratsd, results='asis'}
tab_print(SD_Results %>% select(Stratifier, Period, Tickers, Ratio) %>%
            pivot_wider(names_from = Tickers, values_from = Ratio) %>%
            select(Stratifier, Period, LargeCaps, MidCaps, SmallCaps, CappedSWIX) %>%
            arrange(Stratifier, Period),
          caption = "Volatility in extreme months relative to the full sample (ratio)",
          label = "tab:stratsd", digits = 2, size = "\\scriptsize")
```

Relative returns, however, depend on **local** stress only (Table \ref{tab:strattt}, Figure \ref{Figure8}).

- **In calm months, large caps lead the market**, beating J433 by 0.7% a month in 68% of months.
- **In turbulent months, the leadership flips.** Mid and small caps beat J433 by about 0.8% a month, while large caps lag in three out of four months.
- **The differences are significant** for large caps ($p = 0.01$) and mid caps ($p = 0.02$).
- **Global stratifiers (VIX, oil, the rand, policy uncertainty) produce no significant size effect** (all $p > 0.19$). Global shocks hit all size segments similarly, so a size tilt is not a hedge against offshore uncertainty.

The small-cap result should be read with the stale-price caveat in mind: lagged prices make falls look smaller. The mid-cap result does not suffer from this.

```{r tab-strattt, results='asis'}
            rename(Index = Tickers, `High minus Low (monthly)` = Diff_Hi_minus_Lo,
                   `p-value` = p_value),
          caption = "Monthly excess return over J433: High minus Low months (Welch t-test)",
          label = "tab:strattt", digits = 4, size = "\\scriptsize")
```


```{r tab-summary, results='asis'}
Summary_Tab <- tibble(
  Technique = c("Sector weights", "Concentration", "Active share",
                "Rolling returns", "Realised volatility", "Stale-price checks",
                "GJR-GARCH", "Stratification"),
  `Large caps` = c("Resources-heavy (35-40%)", "Most concentrated", "Low (15%): close to J433",
                   "Beat J433 in 96% of 3y windows", "Mid-range", "Clean",
                   "Strong bad-news effect", "Lead in calm months"),
  `Mid caps`   = c("Financials rising (28%)", "Rising concentration", "High (75%)",
                   "Beat J433 in 26% of windows", "Mid-range", "Minor",
                   "More symmetric", "Lead in stressed months"),
  `Small caps` = c("Property & Industrials", "Most diversified", "Very high (93%)",
                   "Volatile: -16% to +37% p.a.", "Lowest (index), highest (stocks)",
                   "Strong: vol understated", "Most symmetric", "Lead in stressed months*")
)
print(xtable::xtable(Summary_Tab, caption = "Summary of findings by technique",
                     label = "tab:summary",
                     align = c("l", "p{2.6cm}", "p{3.6cm}", "p{3.6cm}", "p{3.6cm}")),
```

\noindent \footnotesize{* Subject to the stale-price caveat in Section \ref{Vol}.} \normalsize

The three size indexes offer distinct exposures:

- **Large caps** are a concentrated Resources and gold bet that has converged towards the Capped SWIX. They led the market over most of the sample and in calm months, but their volatility reacts sharply to bad news.
- **Mid caps** are a Financials-tilted, increasingly concentrated portfolio far from the benchmark. They underperformed overall but held up best in locally stressed months.
- **Small caps** are the most different from J433 and the most diversified internally. Their low measured volatility is partly a liquidity effect, and their tail risk is the largest.

For a manager benchmarked to the Capped SWIX, mid and small caps are the source of genuine diversification, but against local stress, not offshore uncertainty. Their measured risk should be judged on monthly rather than daily data.

The main limitations are the missing sector labels for small caps, the stocks that sit in both the large- and mid-cap indexes at the same time, and the short sample of extreme months (28 per group) in the stratification.

```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Load data
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Peers     <- read_rds("data/Active_Managers.rds")
ABC       <- read_rds("data/ABC_Fund.rds")
Idx_Daily <- read_rds("data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds")
Stocks    <- read_rds("data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds")
Cons      <- read_rds("data/Monthly_Index_Constituents.rds")

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Monthly benchmark from daily J433 (Bonus 22, Step 2): compound with
# cumprod, take the month-end value, join to funds by YearMonth (YM)
# rather than by date (avoids 28 vs 29 Feb mismatches).
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
BMUse <-
  Idx_Daily %>%
  filter(Tickers == "J433") %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(cp = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  fmxdat::YM() %>%
  group_by(YM) %>%
  filter(date == dplyr::last(date)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(BM = cp / lag(cp) - 1) %>%
  filter(!is.na(BM))       # Jan 2015 has no full-month return

# All funds (peers + ABC), full history
Funds <-
  bind_rows(Peers, ABC) %>%
  rename(Funds = Name) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Returns)) %>%
  fmxdat::YM() %>%
  mutate(Group = ifelse(Funds == "ABC_Fund", "ABC Fund", "Peers"))

# Funds joined to the benchmark (common sample: Feb 2015 - Oct 2025)
active_df <-
  left_join(Funds, BMUse %>% select(YM, BM), by = "YM") %>%
  filter(!is.na(BM))
```

# Introduction

## The four questions we answer

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
**The questions**

1. How much market beta do peers give clients?
2. What drives ABC's returns vs the industry?
3. How has ABC done against peers over time?
4. Does ABC win when dispersion is high?
:::
::: {.column}
**Short answers**

1. A lot (beta 0.8–0.9). ABC has the lowest.
2. The manager, not the market; highest alpha.
3. Mostly top quartile; lagged the 2025 rally.
4. No: ABC's edge is not dispersion-driven.
:::
:::::

::: notes
Open with the questions the audience cares about and give the answers up front. The rest of the deck shows the evidence for each.
:::

# Data

## Data used

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r tab-data}
knitr::kable(Tab_Data)
```
:::
::: {.column}
- Returns only, as reported by the managers; no holdings.
- **Closed funds are kept.** Dropping them would flatter the industry (survivorship bias).
- J433 data start in 2015, so benchmark comparisons cover Feb 2015 to Oct 2025.
:::
:::::

::: notes
Point out that about a third of the funds in the peer universe stopped reporting along the way. Keeping them gives a fair picture of what investors actually experienced.
:::

# Methodology

## How we measure market exposure and skill

- **Beta**: move per 1% market move. **β = Cov(R~fund~, R~J433~) / Var(R~J433~)**, rolling 36 months.
- **R-squared**: share of moves explained by the market. **R² = Corr(R~fund~, R~J433~)²**
- **Alpha**: return after market exposure. **R~fund~ = α + β·R~J433~ + ε**
- **Different bets**: correlation of each fund's leftover return ε with the median peer's.

::: notes
Keep this light for the audience: beta = market sensitivity; R-squared = how much of the fund is just the market; alpha = what the manager added.
:::

## How we measure relative performance and dispersion

- **Peer rank** (Bacon, 2011): **(n − 1) / (N − 1)**, n = ABC's position among N funds; 0% = best.
- **Rolling returns**: 12-month and 3-year returns at every month-end.
- **Dispersion**: **Disp = √( Σ w~i~ (R~i~ − R~J433~)² )**, Capped SWIX weights.
- **High vs low dispersion**: above the 85th vs below the 25th percentile; Welch t-test.

::: notes
Dispersion is the "opportunity set": when stocks move very differently from each other, stock pickers have more room to win or lose.
:::

# Results

```{r beta, include=FALSE}
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Q1: Rolling 36-month beta for every fund
# beta = cov(R, BM) / var(BM) using rolling means (same OLS beta as
# Practical 1's CAPM.beta / chart.RollingRegression, but fast for 240+ funds)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Roll_N <- 36

Roll_Beta <-
  active_df %>%
  group_by(Funds) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  filter(n() >= Roll_N) %>%
  mutate(
    m_R  = roll_mean(Returns,      n = Roll_N, fill = NA, align = "right"),
    m_B  = roll_mean(BM,           n = Roll_N, fill = NA, align = "right"),
    m_RB = roll_mean(Returns * BM, n = Roll_N, fill = NA, align = "right"),
    m_BB = roll_mean(BM^2,         n = Roll_N, fill = NA, align = "right"),
    m_RR = roll_mean(Returns^2,    n = Roll_N, fill = NA, align = "right"),
    Cov  = m_RB - m_R * m_B,
    VarB = m_BB - m_B^2,
    VarR = m_RR - m_R^2,
    Beta = Cov / VarB,
    R2   = Cov^2 / (VarB * VarR),
    # require 36 consecutive months (no gaps in the fund's history)
    Gap_ok = as.numeric(date - lag(date, Roll_N - 1)) < (Roll_N + 1) * 31
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(Beta), Gap_ok) %>%
  select(date, YM, Funds, Group, Beta, R2)

# Boxplot over scatter at each year-end
Beta_YE <- Roll_Beta %>% filter(month(date) == 12 | date == max(date)) %>%
  mutate(Year = factor(year(date)))

g_beta <-
  ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = Beta_YE %>% filter(Group == "Peers"),
              aes(Year, Beta), width = 0.2, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.5,
              color = "grey40") +
  geom_boxplot(data = Beta_YE %>% filter(Group == "Peers"),
               aes(Year, Beta), alpha = 0.4, outlier.shape = NA,
               fill = "steelblue", width = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = Beta_YE %>% filter(Group == "ABC Fund"),
             aes(Year, Beta), color = "darkred", size = 4, shape = 18) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Rolling 3-year beta to the Capped SWIX",
       subtitle = "Grey dots = peer funds; box = middle 50% of peers; red diamond = ABC Fund",
       x = "", y = "Rolling 36-month beta",
       caption = "Note:\nMeasured at each year-end (2025 = October). Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE)

Beta_Summary <-
  Beta_YE %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  summarise(`Peer median` = median(Beta[Group == "Peers"]),
            `Peers above 0.9` = mean(Beta[Group == "Peers"] > 0.9),
            `ABC beta` = Beta[Group == "ABC Fund"][1],
            `Peers with higher beta than ABC` = mean(Beta[Group == "Peers"] > `ABC beta`))

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Q2: single-factor model per fund (funds with 5+ years of data)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
SFM <-
  active_df %>%
  group_by(Funds, Group) %>%
  filter(n() >= 60) %>%
  summarise(Months    = n(),
            Beta      = cov(Returns, BM) / var(BM),
            R2        = cor(Returns, BM)^2,
            Alpha_Ann = (1 + mean(Returns - Beta * BM))^12 - 1,
            TE        = sd(Returns - BM) * sqrt(12),
            .groups = "drop")

# ABC vs median peer, plus ABC's percentile among peers (all as text for the slide)
ABC_Row  <- SFM %>% filter(Group == "ABC Fund")
Peer_SFM <- SFM %>% filter(Group == "Peers") %>%
  summarise(across(c(Beta, R2, Alpha_Ann, TE), median))
ABC_Pctl <- SFM %>%
  summarise(across(c(Beta, R2, Alpha_Ann, TE),
                   ~mean(.[Group == "Peers"] < .[Group == "ABC Fund"])))

SFM_Table <- tibble(
  Measure          = c("Beta", "R-squared", "Alpha (ann.)", "Tracking error"),
  `ABC Fund`       = c(round(ABC_Row$Beta, 2), pct(ABC_Row$R2), pct(ABC_Row$Alpha_Ann), pct(ABC_Row$TE)),
  `Median peer`    = c(round(Peer_SFM$Beta, 2), pct(Peer_SFM$R2), pct(Peer_SFM$Alpha_Ann), pct(Peer_SFM$TE)),
  `ABC percentile` = pct(unlist(ABC_Pctl), 1)
)

g_drivers <-
  SFM %>%
  ggplot(aes(R2, Beta)) +
  geom_point(data = . %>% filter(Group == "Peers"), alpha = 0.5,
             color = "grey40", size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = . %>% filter(Group == "ABC Fund"), color = "darkred",
             size = 5, shape = 18) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(SFM$R2[SFM$Group == "Peers"]), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "What drives returns: market vs manager",
       subtitle = "Red diamond = ABC Fund; dashed line = median peer R-squared",
       x = "R-squared vs Capped SWIX (share explained by the market)", y = "Beta",
       caption = "Note:\nMonthly returns, funds with 5+ years of data, 2015-2025. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Q2b: are ABC's bets different? Correlate market-adjusted returns
# (residuals from R = a + b*BM) with the median peer's residual.
# Raw active returns would mislead: all low-beta funds lag in rallies.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
Resid_df <-
  active_df %>%
  group_by(Funds, Group) %>%
  filter(n() >= 60) %>%
  mutate(Resid = residuals(lm(Returns ~ BM))) %>%
  ungroup()

Industry_Resid <-
  Resid_df %>% filter(Group == "Peers") %>%
  group_by(YM) %>%
  summarise(Ind_Resid = median(Resid))

Resid_Corr <-
  Resid_df %>%
  left_join(Industry_Resid, by = "YM") %>%
  group_by(Funds, Group) %>%
  summarise(Corr_with_Industry = cor(Resid, Ind_Resid), .groups = "drop")

ABC_Corr      <- Resid_Corr$Corr_with_Industry[Resid_Corr$Group == "ABC Fund"]
Peer_Med_Corr <- median(Resid_Corr$Corr_with_Industry[Resid_Corr$Group == "Peers"])
ABC_Corr_Pct  <- mean(Resid_Corr$Corr_with_Industry[Resid_Corr$Group == "Peers"] < ABC_Corr)

g_xscorr <-
  ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(data = Resid_Corr %>% filter(Group == "Peers"),
                 aes(Corr_with_Industry), bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = Resid_Corr %>% filter(Group == "ABC Fund"),
             aes(xintercept = Corr_with_Industry), color = "darkred", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "How similar are managers' own bets to the industry's?",
       subtitle = "Correlation with the median peer's market-adjusted return (red line = ABC)",
       x = "Correlation", y = "Number of funds",
       caption = "Note:\nMarket-adjusted return = residual from a regression on the Capped SWIX. Source: own calculations.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = TRUE)
```

## Most active managers give clients mostly market beta

- The typical peer's 3-year beta sits at **about 0.8–0.9** every year.
- **Roughly a third to a half** of peers have beta above 0.9: close to an index fund, at active fees.
- **ABC's beta fell from 0.72 to 0.40**: by 2025 it is the lowest-beta fund in the peer group.

## ABC's returns are driven by the manager, not the market

:::
